Map: Here are the countries that allow for birthright citizenship Updated: 11:53 AM CDT Apr 1, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ More than 30 countries allow for unrestricted birthright citizenship, including, for now, the U.S. On Wednesday, the Supreme Court heard arguments about President Donald Trump's executive order, issued last year on the first day of his second term, that calls to end automatic birthright citizenship.Birthright citizenship means that a person born in a country, regardless of their parents' immigration status, is automatically a citizen of that country. It is protected in the U.S. by the 14th Amendment.Most of the countries that allow for birthright citizenship are concentrated in North and South America. Both U.S. neighbors, Canada and Mexico, allow unrestricted birthright citizenship, as do all but two countries in South America. In the Eastern Hemisphere, Lesotho, Tanzania and Pakistan are among the countries that grant automatic citizenship to those born on their soil. Wanted to know if you pay to pick your seat and the airline moves you to another seat, are you owed money for that? The answer, it depends based on how you book. When you book *** flight in economy, not first class, not the extra legroom option, you will usually see the fare broken down into options like basic and standard. Different airlines call standard different things, but the breakdown itself. It is pretty universal. Standard is usually more expensive, includes advanced seat selection in the price, and often comes with other perks like earlier boarding and earning miles. With basic, the cheaper option, seat selection is not bundled into the price. You have to pay extra, otherwise your seat is assigned for you. Now, if you pick your seat and the airline moves you, these two tickets are. Treated very differently, and this actually might surprise you. Under Department of Transportation rules, airlines owe you money in two cases. First, downgrades. If you book first class but yet moved to economy, you're owed the difference if you continue on the flight. Second, if you paid *** fee for an optional add-on not included in the price of your ticket. So let's go back to those two examples we talked about for ***. So let's say you booked *** window seat and the airline made you move to *** middle seat. Well, if you booked that standard ticket, you're actually not owed *** refund because seat selection was already bundled into the price. Even though you might have paid more than the basic fare, in the DOT's eyes, you technically didn't pay *** fee. It's also not considered *** downgrade since you're still in the same cabin. But if you booked *** basic ticket, you did pay *** fee to pick your seat. So if the airline moves you, you should get that fee refunded back to you. In the case of Nicole, whose TikTok we showed you earlier, she caught the switch up early enough to contact United, and she tells me she got them to move her back to her original seat. Who is making these calls? Bottom line, make sure you pay attention to what all is included in your ticket. If perks like miles matter to you, booking standard may still be the best option, but it's worth making sure you run the numbers. Reporting in New York, I'm Ali Jasinski. Ask Allie: Are you owed a refund when airlines change your seat? The way you book your flight can impact your consumer protections, including whether you get a refund if your seat is changed. Updated: 12:01 PM CDT Apr 14, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ It can be frustrating: You pick a seat on a flight, only to have the airline move you to a different one.So, are you owed a refund? The answer depends on how you booked your ticket.How airline tickets are structured When booking an economy flight — not first class or extra legroom options — passengers are typically presented with multiple fare options, often labeled "Basic Economy" and "Standard," though names vary by airline.For example, United Airlines offers Basic Economy and United Economy Standard, while American Airlines offers Basic Economy and Main Cabin.The higher-priced option generally includes perks such as:Advance seat selectionEarlier boardingThe ability to earn frequent flyer milesThe cheaper basic option typically does not include seat selection. Passengers who choose these fares are often assigned a seat unless they pay an additional fee to select one in advance.When you are owed a refundUnder U.S. Department of Transportation rules, airlines are required to issue refunds in certain situations.One is a downgrade. If a passenger pays for a higher class, like first class, but is moved to a lower class, like economy, and still takes the flight, the airline must refund the difference in fare. Another applies to optional add-ons, known as ancillary services. These are services not included in the base ticket price, such as paying a separate fee to select a specific seat. So, let's go back to that Standard vs. Basic ticket.The catch with bundled seat selection If a passenger books a standard or main cabin fare where seat selection is included in the ticket price, that feature is considered part of the bundle — not a separate purchase.That means if a passenger selects a window seat but is later moved to a middle seat, federal rules generally do not require the airline to issue a refund. That's because:The seat selection was not purchased as a separate feeThe passenger remains in the same cabin, so it is not considered a downgradeHowever, if a passenger books a lower-cost basic ticket and pays an additional fee to select that same seat, they may be entitled to a refund if the airline does not provide it. What travelers should know Before booking, review what is included in your ticket and how services are priced.Higher-tier fares may offer convenience and perks, but separately paid add-ons can come with stronger refund protections.If an airline changes your seat, it may still be worth contacting customer service. Carnes. ‘Cocaine hippos’ linked to drug lord Pablo Escobar will be euthanized Updated: 3:36 PM CDT Apr 15, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Colombian officials on Monday authorized a plan to cull dozens of hippos roaming freely through a region in the center of the country, where they threaten villagers and displace native species years after notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar brought in the first ones.Environment Minister Irene Vélez said previous methods to control their population have been expensive and unsuccessful, including neutering some of the animals or moving them to zoos. Vélez said up to 80 hippos would be affected by the measure. She did not say when hunting would begin.“If we don’t do this we will not be able to control the population,” Vélez said. “We have to take this action to preserve our ecosystems.”Colombia is the only country outside of Africa with a wild hippo population. Dubbed "cocaine hippos," the wild hippos are the descendants of four brought to the country in the 1980s by Escobar as he built a private zoo in Hacienda Nápoles, a gigantic ranch in the Magdalena River valley with a private landing strip that served as his rural abode.A study published by Colombia’s National University estimated that around 170 hippos were roaming freely in the country in 2022.Recently, hippos have been spotted in areas that are more than 60 miles north of the ranch.Environmental authorities in Colombia say the mammals pose a threat to villagers who have encountered them in farms and rivers. They also compete for food and space against local species such as river manatees.Despite the challenges, the hippos have also become a tourist attraction, with residents of villages surrounding Hacienda Nápoles offering hippo spotting tours and selling hippo-themed souvenirs.The hippos are also one of the main attractions at the Nápoles ranch, which was confiscated by Colombia’s government as it seized Escobar’s properties. It now functions as a theme park, featuring swimming spools, water slides and a zoo that includes several other African species.Animal welfare activists in Colombia have long opposed proposals to kill the hippos, arguing they deserve to live. They say that addressing the problem through violence sets a poor example for a country that has gone through decades of internal conflict.Andrea Padilla, a senator and animal rights activist who helped draft a law against bullfights in Colombia, described the plan to cull the hippos as a “cruel” decision, and accused government officials of trying to take the easy way out.“Killings and massacres will never be acceptable,” Padilla wrote on X. “These are healthy creatures who are victims of the negligence” of government entities.Over the past 12 years, spanning three presidential administrations, Colombia has tried to neuter some of the hippos in a bid to reduce their population. But the initiatives have had limited scope due to high costs that come with capturing the dangerous animals and performing surgeries on them.Because Colombia’s hippos come from a limited gene pool and could carry diseases, taking them back to their natural habitat in Africa has been considered unfeasible. THE FINAL CERTIFICATION DECISION WILL BE MADE AFTER COGNIA COMPLETES ITS FORMAL REPORT AND SUBMITS THE RECOMMENDATION TO Tuscaloosa City Schools first in world recommended for global board certification Updated: 6:33 PM CDT Apr 15, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Tuscaloosa City Schools has made history as the first school system in the world to be recommended for board certification by Cognia, a global accrediting organization that works with school boards in more than 100 countries. The recommendation follows several days of interviews, document reviews, and observations conducted by Cognia. Eric Wilson, chairman of the Tuscaloosa City Schools Board of Education, said the process demonstrates the district's dedication to its students. "We really wanted the process itself to look introspectively and learn and grow," Wilson said. During the review, Cognia's team interviewed 65 individuals, including board members, administrators, principals, teachers, parents, and community members. Cognia’s deputy chief of accreditation services said the consistency in responses stood out during the evaluation. "It's an objective look and an objective analysis of all the hard work that we as a board and, more importantly, the system have been doing for ten years, really, and it's been a long time," Wilson said. The review highlighted several strengths of the school system, including strong collaboration between the board and district leadership and a clear focus on student success and equity. Wilson hopes the report will emphasize the board’s commitment to the Tuscaloosa community. "I think the community will have something to say, 'Wow. Our board really loves our city, really loves our system, really loves our students, and they are going to do everything in their power and work really hard to make sure that we are going above and beyond for our system and our students,'" Wilson said. He added that the certification aligns with the board's data-driven approach to decision-making. "We're a very data-driven board. They love that. We will continue to be data-driven. It drives our decisions, whether that's academic programs, whether that's budgetary decisions. We don't stop if we get this honor. It will just embolden us to continue to work harder," Wilson said. The final certification decision will be made after Cognia completes its formal report and submits the recommendation to its global commission for approval, a process expected to take several weeks.
